newsitem.title: USA: Wall St stocks seen opening sharply lower.
newsitem.headline: Wall St stocks seen opening sharply lower.

text.p: U.S. stocks are expected to meet with heavy selling at Wednesday's open, pressured by a series of reports and rumors that called into question the recent strength of blue chips and technology stocks.

Analysts said the market, which has again showed fierce resilience following a sharp sell-off last Friday, would be tested once more by rumors International Business Machines Corp was about to issue a profit warning and a column in today's Wall Street Journal questioning whether Japanese institutions were losing their appetite for U.S. Treasuries.
"It looks like a very rough morning," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities.

Regarding the Wall Street Journal report, which appeared in its Heard on the Street column, Wachtel said, "We've seen these stories time and time again, but because this one comes from (Goldman Sachs International Vice Chairman Robert) Hormats it carries some weight."
U.S. Treasuries were weaker in early activity, with the 30-year bond off 20/32 to yield 6.54 percent.
Analysts said blue chips and techs were vulnerable to a corrective sell-off because of their recent strength.
Perhaps most vulnerable is IBM, which has staged a huge rally in the past month.
"There are grumblings about an IBM earnings warning," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, "and it's clear IBM would be clobbered if that's the case."
"I expect a sharply lower opening and I would not rule out a drop like Friday," he said "It's possible we could see the Dow dropping as much as 150 points during the day."
All but overshadowed was the release of the November Producer Price Index, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
Economists expect a 0.3 percent increase and a 0.2 percent rise in the core rate, which excludes food and energy.
In Tokyo, stocks settled lower after two days of strong gains. The Nikkei-225 index fell 254 points to 20,568.
U.S. shares edged down in London, with trading in IBM shares coming to a virtual halt. The FTSE-100 fell 53.5 points to 3982.2.
The dollar eased in Tokyo after a surprise interest rate cut by the Reserve Bank of Australia. The greenback was steady near session lows in Europe ahead of release of the PPI.
The December Standard & Poor's 500 index future fell 6.7 points to 741.3.

The New York Times Marketplace column focuses on a rally in Chinese dollar-denominated shares. The class B shares, originally intended only for international investors, are now being gobbled up by Chinese investors thanks to looser rules enforcement, the column said.
